extracted.intended_audience: faculty and principal investigators considering whether to revise and resubmit a declined research grant proposal (especially early-career faculty applying to federal agencies)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for analyzing reviewer feedback on a declined research proposal and deciding whether and how to revise and resubmit, including concrete steps for diagnosing weaknesses, planning revisions, and interacting with program officers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Review your ratings carefully
rubrics_metrics.description: The first question you should ask yourself is, what were your ratings? Can they be trusted?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Two or more “good” and even one “fair” (or a “no score” at NIH) is a genuine death sentence. Bi-modal reviews (e.g., E, VG, E, G, F, P) or outlier reviews (all high scores except 1 fair or poor) have special dynamics: these are almost always discussed to ascertain an appropriate rating, but once even one review is negative it is very hard to overcome its influence. Scores are one of many indicators derived from reviewer comments; understand the context and meaning of scores and associated review comments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Focus on weaknesses, not positives
rubrics_metrics.description: It is unhelpful to look at the positive comments. Focus instead, only on weaknesses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: You are seeking to understand if there was a critical flaw in the fundamental premise or a collection of minor weaknesses. Concentrate on criticisms that explain the scores rather than flattering comments that don't indicate fixable problems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Categorize reviewer weaknesses (novelty, capabilities, specific criteria)
rubrics_metrics.description: All weaknesses typically fall into the following three categories: Novelty or intellectual contribution; Capabilities to carry out the work; Specific review criteria (nuances of program types like NSF CAREER, NIH AREA).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Novelty: proposal fails to 'move the needle' or address an important gap. Capabilities: methodological plans, missing skills/resources, or lack of confidence in PI's ability. Specific review criteria: failure to tailor approach to program-specific expectations. Use this taxonomy to diagnose the root cause(s) of the decline.

rubrics_metrics.name: Test the validity of stated weaknesses
rubrics_metrics.description: First, ask yourself about the validity of the weaknesses. Were the reviewers right?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be honest; answer yes or no. If you feel they were not right, get a second or third opinion. Be prepared to address prior weaknesses when you do resubmit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assess criticality: fatal vs. fixable weaknesses
rubrics_metrics.description: If the identified weakness struck a fatal blow to Intellectual Merit (IM), novelty, or hypothesis, the proposal is not viable until you refine the core idea.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A flaw in IM is 'equivalent to heart failure.' If the flaws are in methods, determine whether they can be corrected and where (methods, personnel, management). Many methodological critiques can be overcome by acknowledging reviewers' perspectives and explaining why your approach is the best choice given alternatives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Determine fixability of methodological/personnel/management issues
rubrics_metrics.description: For methodological weaknesses, ask a) if they can be corrected and b) where exactly they occurred (methods, personnel, management).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Most non-critical weaknesses are in methodology. If fixes are feasible (e.g., adding personnel, clarifying techniques/statistics), document how you'll change the plan. Acknowledge reviewer concerns and justify chosen methods relative to alternatives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Create a weaknesses-only review matrix
rubrics_metrics.description: Take each weakness from each review, across all reviews, OUT of the context of the individual review, and list them together in a new 'weaknesses only' review matrix.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Removing reviewer context allows de novo analysis. Examine weaknesses on their own merits and in combination; relate one weakness to another to look for patterns. Distinguish more important from less important weaknesses to prioritize fixes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Correct stylistic and presentation weaknesses
rubrics_metrics.description: If your proposal’s weaknesses were stylistic in nature, get help to correct them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Find a good proposal writer or editor to improve clarity; clearer conveyance of key ideas can make reviews more accurate and reduce 'middle-of-the-road' ambiguous reviews caused by excellent presentation but unclear substance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Check resubmission limits and agency policies
rubrics_metrics.description: Remember to check for any resubmission limits of the funding agency.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Some agencies or programs limit resubmissions or have special policies; confirm whether you can revise and resubmit and in what timeframe before deciding on a course of action.

rubrics_metrics.name: When revising, address only validated criticisms and avoid creating new weaknesses
rubrics_metrics.description: As you revise and resubmit, make sure you address only validated criticisms and do not create additional weaknesses or miss weaknesses that reviewers failed to mention previously.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mid-range proposals may have undiscovered weaknesses; fixing one set may reveal others. Revise thoroughly—resubmit efforts can take 25–40 additional hours, almost like creating a new proposal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider alternative funding sources and retrofitting
rubrics_metrics.description: If not resubmitting immediately, keep the declined proposal 'on ice' or retrofit it for other funding sources (e.g., private foundations).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check alternative sources and tailor the project to fit their priorities. A declined federal application may be a good fit elsewhere with adjustments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consult the program officer for fit and validation
rubrics_metrics.description: Check with your program officer to see if the proposal is still a good fit and to validate your analysis of the reviews.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Program officers can help validate key weaknesses you uncovered in your matrix and can flag unfair or ad hominem reviews; they cannot discuss specifics of panel deliberations but can advise on fit and next steps.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize panel dynamics and protections against unfair reviews
rubrics_metrics.description: Program officers and chairs ensure good review panel practices and can ask that unfair or ad hominem comments be tagged and not considered in decisions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because of these safeguards, most proposal reviews are fair and hard to prove unfairness; avoid blaming reviewers and take criticism as a learning opportunity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Understand that scores are contextual and funding decisions can change
rubrics_metrics.description: Even all positive scores can sometimes result in a declination; external changes (e.g., new funding streams) can later lead to previously declined proposals being funded.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Scores are one indicator among many derived from reviewer comments; use context to assess revivability. Historical example: NSF 'un-declined' proposals after AARA stimulus, showing scores alone don't fully determine outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: If not resubmitting, conduct a post-mortem and use coping strategies
rubrics_metrics.description: If you decide not to revise or resubmit, conduct an in-depth post-mortem analysis of the reviews to learn from mistakes and understand options.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the post-mortem to improve future proposals, process feedback constructively, and manage the emotional impact of declination.
